Event[0] is a game that has very unfortunately been negatively impacted by AI becoming more prominent in everyday life. This is, obviously, through no fault of the developers!

Sometimes games hinge on a core element, like graphical fidelity, or a unique gimmick. If the landscape of the world changes so that that gimmick or quality is no longer outstanding, no longer unique? The entire piece of media can totally fall flat. Games made in the early 2000s to show off the current capabilities of technology can look sort of silly to modern audiences.

I played Event[0] before LLMs were really around in any meaningful way, and as a result, the interactive elements of speaking to a character through a dialogue box? It was gripping, and helped me maintain interest and keep pushing through the rest of the game. This is certainly by design - you are not offered much to keep your attention grabbed at first, other than the opportunity to have a chat with a fictional AI. Nowadays, this is not only a less intriguing and inviting concept, but it is also done better - Event[0]'s AI is not a LLM, and as a result, kind of awkwardly and obtusely ignores or redirects what you say. That artifice really worked in a pre-chatGPT world, but unfortunately now, it leads a player to immediately see through the ruse. To immediately be able to see past the very well crafted curtains that once hid the innerworkings and limitations of this gameplay gimmick.

That said, Event[0] is still a good game AROUND its gimmick, which is why I'm still recommending it. It may have lost a fair deal of its unique pizzazz in the eyes of a modern player, but the visuals, the music, and the story are still very engaging and so the game is still an absolute treat to play through.

I had a bit of a hard time trying to decide how to review this game, as my experience was a bit mixed. On one hand, the game looks fantastic, which a beautifully designed space station to explore, and the premise of the game which involves exploring an abandoned space station is right up my alley as well. Unfortunately, I have three major gripes with the way this game plays out:

[list]
[*] The game is really short. I played through the game twice, and it took me 3 hours each time. I tend to spend a lot of time exploring everywhere and reading everything too, so most people will probably beat this game in an hour or two. Given the price, that's really not a lot of playtime.
[*] The story is a bit hard to follow, especially if you don't spend the time to read everything. The narrative is primarily told through the logs you find on the computer and the responses you're given by Kaizen, the terminal AI. Unfortunately, the logs are "corrupted", which means you have to sift through loads of empty logs, and the ones that are there are often missing sections, making them hard to understand. Kaizen givens you narrative during your interactions with him as well, but...
[*] Kaizen can be very frustrating to interact with, and since he's a major source of lore and the primary way you play the game, this makes the game feel like a bit of a chore. When Kaizen perfectly answers your questions, the game feels really cool, but I found those interactions to be fairly rare, and most of my questions were obviously misunderstood or outright rejected by Kaizen. Almost every interaction with him involved asking the same question over and over, trying to find the right wording for Kaizen to understand what I wanted, which was not enjoyable.
[/list]

The game ran well and looks fantastic. Outside of the frustration with Kaizen, I didn't run into any bugs or other issues while playing.

[b]TL;DR[/b] This space adventure game has a beautiful environment and a really cool premise, but has an extremely short playtime, has a fragmented story that can be quite sparse and challenging to understand, and the interactions with Kaizen leave a lot to be desired and often lead to frustration. I imagine there are probably some people who will still enjoy this game, but given these issues, I just can't recommend it.

Really interesting stuff. 

The gameplay itself was simple but engaging. However there were times I got confused and didn't know how to proceed. There is a built in hint system [spoiler](by talking to Kaizen-85)[/spoiler] but it can be difficult to get the information that you want. Particularly the part immediately after my first foray into the [spoiler]garden[/spoiler] had me confused as to what to do with the info I had. Then, once I understood what I needed to do, I didn't remember how I was supposed to do it. (because that was info I received so much earlier that I had largely forgotten)

Also the music. How have I not said something about it yet. There's not much, but what is there works so well and sounds amazing.

Overall, I think it's a solid showcase of it's gameplay systems.

Free-typing as a prominent mechanic was REALLY FUN, which surprised me. Most of the time my interactions with Kaizen were legitimately engaging. Since you could say anything to Kaizen, I didn't ever mentally check out like I sometimes do when provided preset dialogue options. 

The puzzles aren't really logic puzzles - they're more about being perceptive and making some clever mental connections. This linear puzzle style might crumble in a longer game, but it was a nice fit in such a short experience.

这是一个非常独特的假AI驱动的游戏，在大模型层出的今天看来kaizen并不是真正的AI，哪怕kaizen设计的回答字句再多，作者再用心，由于玩家的想象力是近乎无限的，也就无法避免答非所问情况的时常发生。而这个情况也一定程度上会让玩家失望，因为如果一个人工智能被发现是人工智障人们必定会失望，结果玩到后面玩家就知道其实这只是需要你说出特定表达来触发剧情推动的游戏而已，期待程度会大大降低。

然而，如果你抛开kaizen这个假AI的问题不谈，就玩法和剧情来说整个游戏依然在所有解谜游戏里是独一份的存在，到后来了解anele和nandi的事之后你会去思考，搭配孤独的氛围营造，你必然会细思极恐。在kaizen试图把你拦在舱外的时候看得出来，作者想让你觉得你面对的不是一个友善的可爱AI，而是第二个能够尝试将你置于死地的哈尔9000。而你也需要作出你的选择，无关对错的选择。作为一个科幻迷我无疑很喜欢这款游戏，哪怕游戏流程的确很短。
